candidates.context: Results from controlled trials of antihypertensive drugs show that decreases in blood pressure led 66 to decreased rates of stroke and cardiovascular deaths in populations with all levels of risk from 67 other factors, such as elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol or smoking status. 68 Maintenance of a reduction in blood pressure with antihypertensive drug regimens consistently 69 reduced rates of stroke and cardiovascular death, with a less consistent effect on nonfatal 70 myocardial infarction (see Table 1 in the Appendix). Furthermore, the beneficial effect on 71 cardiovascular outcome occurs within a relatively short period of time (0.5 to 1 year), suggesting 72 that an increased risk from elevated blood pressure would also occur relatively rapidly (Staessen 73 et al. 1997; Veterans Administration Cooperative Study 1970). candidates.statement: There is greater concern with the effects of a drug on blood pressure when the drug will be used 134 chronically. As noted above, the risk related to blood pressure is a continuous function, and 135 sustained increases in blood pressure correlate with long-term increases in the risk of 136 cardiovascular events. It follows that drug-induced sustained elevations in blood pressure, even if 137 small, would have such effects. Sponsors, therefore, should include a thorough blood pressure 138 assessment for any drug intended for chronic use. FDA recommends use of ABPM for this 139 assessment, as ABPM is capable of detecting small, but potentially relevant, blood pressure 140 effects (see section IV). ABPM also assesses effects over a 24-hour period, which is more 141 informative than assessment at a single time point (Pickering 2000). 142
candidates.context: B. Drugs Intended for Chronic Use 132 IV. TYPES OF BLOOD PRESSURE ASSESSMENT 145

candidates.statement: The accuracy of clinic blood pressure measurement can be improved by collecting triplicate 154 measurements of sitting blood pressure in all subjects at baseline (predose), at several visits (at 155 least two visits before the end of the trial), at the end of the interdosing interval (trough 156 measurement; predose), and at peak concentration of test drug or active metabolites. 157 Measurements should be made approximately 1 to 3 minutes apart, using the same arm at each 158 visit. For studies with entrance criteria that include specific blood pressure ranges or cutoffs, 159 separate predose measurements should be obtained; screening measurements should not be used 160 as the baseline. 161
candidates.context: Clinic blood pressure measurements can be used for three purposes: to assess the effects of drugs 149 intended for short-term use, to characterize the dose or exposure-response relationship for drugs 150 that increase blood pressure, and to serve as part of the overall safety assessment to identify 151 patients with large increases in blood pressure. 152 If a large blood pressure effect is not detected by clinical blood pressure measurements in early, 163 small studies, FDA recommends an ABPM study for drugs intended to be used chronically. 164

candidates.statement: The ABPM study should be performed in the patient population for which the drug is being 216 developed, either in a targeted study or as part of a larger study already being conducted for other 217 purposes. The study may also be performed in a related patient population with characteristics 218 similar to those of the intended target patient population (i.e., similar demographic and disease- 219 specific characteristics). 220

In general, the study should be powered to exclude a 3-mmHg increase in 24-hour average 224 systolic blood pressure using an upper bound of the two-sided 95% confidence interval assuming 225 the true effect is 0 mmHg. Such an increase would lead to an increase of approximately 0.5 to 1 226 cardiovascular event per 1,000 patient years in patients with intermediate to high cardiovascular 227 risk at baseline (see Figure 1) using the ASCVD risk model. Sponsors and the review division 228 should consider the underlying cardiovascular risk in the patient population and the perceived 229 benefit of the drug when selecting an appropriate effect to be ruled out. 230
candidates.context: Blood pressure should be measured at least twice an hour over 24 hours using ABPM at baseline 232 and on-treatment to assess the overall effect; on-treatment measurements should be performed 233 only after the drug has reached its steady state effect on blood pressure. Based on a meta-analysis 234 of antihypertensive agents, which showed that maximal effect was not observed until 4 weeks of 235 treatment, we recommend that ABPM trials be of at least 4 weeks’ duration (Lasserson et al. 236 2011). 237

candidates.statement: In general, sponsors should present the results as 24-hour average as well as the daytime (awake) 239 and nighttime (asleep) averages. Other presentations may be appropriate depending on the 240 mechanism of action and the expected pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of the 241 drug. Results may suggest that blood pressure elevations are related to drug concentration 242 exposure, which could, in turn, relate to dose and dosing interval. Sponsors should collect 243 pharmacokinetic samples at appropriate time points in an effort to demonstrate treatment 244 compliance and to explore the relationship between blood pressure increases and drug exposure. 245

candidates.statement: Large drug-induced elevations in blood pressure are relevant for all drugs, even for those 256 intended for short-term use. Smaller sustained elevations of blood pressure of even a few 257 millimeters of mercury are a concern when the drug is intended for chronic use, particularly 258 when the target population is at increased cardiovascular risk. As noted above, the increment in 259 proportional risk for a given blood pressure increase appears to be similar across the range of 260 blood pressures, including normal blood pressure. Conversely, the increase in absolute risk 261 would be very small for a person at low baseline risk (e.g., age 25, normal low-density 262 lipoprotein and high-density lipoprotein, not diabetic, and normotensive) and becomes 263 progressively greater as the number and severity of risk factors increase, as shown in Figure 1. 264 Sponsors should consider Figure 1 when formulating their approach to assessing the importance 265 of the pressor effect of a particular drug. 266
candidates.context: VI. REGULATORY RISK ASSESSMENT 254 The finding that a drug increases blood pressure and the magnitude and pattern of that increase 268 should be factored into the overall risk assessment for the drug. This assessment should include 269 consideration of any steps that could be taken to mitigate the risk of increased blood pressure, 270 such as patient selection, pretreatment assessments, blood pressure monitoring in some or all 271 patients, and expectant use of blood pressure–lowering treatments. 272
